title: Don't eat each other's wealth
hookLine: don't consume one another's property unjustly (2:188)
last: NEAR, IN THE MIDDLE OF THE FAST.

lines: YOUR OWN BREAD, UNTOUCHED UNTIL SUNSET.
cards: All day in Ramadan, a fasting person doesn't touch food that is completely theirs. Their own bread, their own water, in their own kitchen, and still they wait for sunset. Now turn the page.
The verse right after the fasting passage isn't about food at all. It's about other people's money.
Some readers see a lesson in the order: if you can hold back all day from what is yours, you can hold back from what isn't. Today: don't eat each other's wealth.

teach.b: Verse one hundred eighty-eight says: do not consume one another's wealth among yourselves falsely, and don't take it to the judges, so that you may knowingly consume a portion of other people's wealth in sin.
The verb is eat. Arabic, like English slang, talks about eating money: swallowing it, devouring it.
The word for falsely is bil-batil: by what is empty, vain, without real right. Cheating, theft, fraud, gambling, a contract with a trick in it: commentators put all of them under this word.
Then the verse names one trap: going to court to make the wrong thing look legal. A bribe to a judge. A clever argument that wins what you know isn't yours.
Bukhari and Muslim preserve a hadith that goes straight at this.
Umm Salamah reported that the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ told people bringing him a dispute: I am only human. One of you may argue his case better than the other, and I judge by what I hear.

If I rule for someone something that is his brother's right, let him not take it. I am only cutting him a piece of the Fire. Even the Prophet's verdict, the hadith says, doesn't make a wrong thing clean.

teach.h: THE COURT CAN BE FOOLED; YOU KNOW
teach.b: The court can be fooled. The one taking it knows; the verse says knowingly.

how: Islamic law forbids taking wealth by fraud, bribery, gambling or unjust contracts, and Muslims are taught to settle debts promptly; many cite 2:188 and the hadith of the piece of Fire when speaking of honest dealing.

o: the empty, the false: what has no real right
a fine paid to a judge to settle a case
a fair trade both sides freely agreed to

p: making the wrong thing look legal
the Prophet on his own verdicts
what a wrongly won case gives you

s: the verse after the fasting passage is about money
2:188: don't consume one another's wealth falsely.
if a court rules in your favor, the wealth is yours, even if you know it isn't
the hadith: it's only a piece of the Fire.

games.q: you argued your case well, and the Prophet himself ruled for you. but you know the thing is really your brother's. what does the hadith say?
o: don't take it; it's a piece of the Fire.
games.why: don't take it. I am only human, he said; a ruling based on clever words doesn't make a wrong thing clean.

practice: Look honestly at what you're holding that isn't fully yours: ten dollars a friend covered at lunch, a tool borrowed months ago, a payment you're late on, change you were given too much of.
Pick one, and picture handing it back with a simple sentence: I owe you this.

wordCard.voice: Batil. The void, the empty, the without-right — what al-Baqarah says not to use in taking another's wealth, even through a clever court case. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: falsely, by what is empty or without right; from batil, the void, the false.

carryVoice: Your line: clean hands. They begin with what you already know is someone else's. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 7169; Sahih Muslim 1713 (Umm Salamah: I am only human; a piece of the Fire)
